item.title: Biden ripped for ‘totally delusional’ claim about debate that preceded his 2024 exit
item.description: Joe Biden tells People Magazine his disastrous June 2024 presidential debate against Trump was "not very consequential," drawing sharp criticism.
item.content:encoded:
Former President Joe Biden is facing sharp backlash after dismissing his disastrous 2024 debate performance against President Donald Trump as "not very consequential" — despite dropping out of the presidential race just 24 days later.

When asked about what his "perspective" on the June 27, 2024 debate is now in an interview with People Magazine released Wednesday, Biden suggested he felt his debate performance was inconsequential.

"Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate," Biden told People Magazine. "To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t."

JILL BIDEN SAYS SHE THOUGHT JOE WAS HAVING A STROKE DURING HIS DISASTROUS 2024 DEBATE PERFORMANCE

"But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential," he added.

Biden's comments drew swift criticism on social media on Wednesday.

SOCIAL MEDIA ERUPTS AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALS SHE WAS 'FRIGHTENED' WATCHING JOE'S DISASTROUS DEBATE

"Joe Biden now claims his 2024 presidential debate against President Trump, which forced him to drop out of the race, was not very consequential," former Trump campaign operative Steve Cortes wrote Wednesday in an X post.

"Just 24 days after the 'not very consequential' presidential debate, Joe Biden ended his campaign for President," Cortes added.

Conservative commentator Steve Guest wrote on X that Biden "is TOTALLY delusional."

Meanwhile, former National Republican Senatorial Committee senior adviser Matt Whitlock asserted in a Wednesday post on X that it was actually "the most consequential" presidential debate of all time.

"It was without question the most consequential Presidential debate in history - he [Biden] likely would have stayed the nominee without it," Whitlock said. "But I’m definitely excited for the other hot takes in the book now."

"It was the most lopsided debate in history. C’mon, man!" Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis quipped.

During the presidential debate, Biden stumbled over his words, paused for long periods of time and displayed confused facial expressions.

The Office of Joe and Jill Biden did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"Biden subsequently dropped out of the presidential race on July 21, 2024, just a few weeks after the debate, amid mounting pressure from Democratic allies to end his re-election bid.

Former first lady Jill Biden notably claimed in a CBS News Sunday Morning interview clip released in May 2026 that she thought her husband was having a stroke on stage during the debate.

Trump's White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Additionally, Biden said Sunday that he plans to scale back public appearances promoting his new presidential memoir, "Promise Me, America," due to his cancer battle.

"My presidential memoir, PROMISE ME, AMERICA, is coming out on November 17th. I hope you'll read it. It covers my years as President. The challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them. It's about who we are as a nation," Biden said in an X post. "What we stand for. And America's role in the world."

"While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families," the former president added. "My doctors continue to be encouraged by how I've responded to treatment. And the prayers and kind words and well wishes from so many of you have meant more to me and Jill and our family than you can ever know. Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down."

item.title: GOP congressman-elect makes unusual Trump request, ejects reporter during profanity-laced victory speech
item.description: Anthony Constantino kicked a reporter out of the room and called on Trump to pardon Diddy during his profanity-laden congressional victory speech.
item.content:encoded:
Anthony Constantino, a former boxer and the CEO of the printing company Sticker Mule, delivered a profanity-laden victory speech after his election to New York’s 21st Congressional District, kicking a reporter out of the room and calling on President Donald Trump to pardon Sean "Diddy" Combs.

"I think President Trump should consider freeing Diddy," Constantino said, referring to the incarcerated producer.

"A historic New Yorker that did great things for New York State. I think we should consider it."

Constantino’s brazen speech contrasts sharply with the demeanor of the district’s outgoing incumbent, Rep. Elise Stefanik, R-N.Y., the former No. 3 Republican in the House of Representatives. It also raises questions about whether Constantino earnestly hopes to see the administration pardon Combs, who was convicted of prostitution across state lines.

DIDDY'S FEDERAL PRISON RELEASE DELAYED WEEKS AFTER REPORTED SOLITARY CONFINEMENT STINT

"Where’s my lawyer at? I have a very good lawyer. Listen, I’m fighting for New York. I want to bring excitement back to New York. I want to bring jobs back to New York," Constantino said moments before his request.

During his 31-minute speech, Constantino spoke about political allies, enemies, the media, power struggles and his vision for the country. He even had a rapper friend perform a freestyle tribute to his congressional election.

At points, Constantino adopted an openly combative tone — especially with respect to members of the press.

"Listen to me, scumbags. Telling people the truth is the right thing to do. I had to listen to you a--holes say ‘dairy farmer Blake Gendebien,’" Constantino said, referring to news coverage of his Democratic challenger.

"He’s not a dairy farmer; his parents were dairy farmers … but you wouldn’t say that because you’re a bunch of f---ing a--holes," he added.

At one point, Constantino singled out a pair of reporters in the crowd.

"Look at that a--hole right there. Him. Look at that guy. Take a picture of him … and Kay Lisa, another f---ing a--hole."

Constantino then ordered one of the reporters removed from the room, describing him as an "angry motherf---er."

ANTIFA SUPPORTER CHARGED WITH STEALING GOP CAMPAIGN SIGNS IN NY RACE TO REPLACE STEFANIK

"Actually, do me a favor. This guy is so — he’s looking at me. Kick him out. Just kick him out. Get him out of here. You’re just a rude person. If you want to be tough on me, get out. Go right now. I’m not playing games with you. You deleted two of my interviews … bye bye," Constantino said.

Stefanik, a former GOP conference chair and Trump’s first pick to become U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, was considered by many a rising star within the Republican Party.

Although Stefanik began the confirmation process for the nomination, Trump ultimately rescinded his pick, calling on Stefanik to remain in the House, where Republicans held a razor-thin majority. A few months later, Stefanik announced that she would not pursue reelection or a bid for governor, citing a desire to focus on her family and avoid a primary contest.

Notably, Stefanik endorsed Constantino after the GOP primary for New York’s 21st Congressional District.

"In the coming months, I know Anthony will continue to work hard to earn your support. He will put the people first and will be a strong representative in Washington for the incredible hardworking families in our great district," Stefanik said in a post to social media.

Constantino also secured backing from President Donald Trump.

Constantino made headlines in 2024 when he put up a giant 100-foot "VOTE FOR TRUMP" sign atop his company building.

City officials, including Democratic Mayor Michael Cinquanti, argued the sign violated code because it "presents a dangerous distraction and impacts traffic flow," especially at night when it is illuminated.

After a legal battle, courts ruled that Constantino had a right to keep the sign in place, a decision he called an "epic win for free speech."

JOHN RICH SAYS KATHY HOCHUL IS ‘RUNNING OVER’ NY FARMERS WITH RENEWABLE ENERGY AGENDA

Last Tuesday, Constantino narrowly won his race in a 50.9% to 48.8% victory over Gendebien.

During his campaign, Constantino stressed his alignment with Trump, highlighting his record as a business owner, promised to bring reliable cell phone service to northern New York and reduce utility costs, according to his website.

Having secured his congressional race, Constantino will be sworn into office on Jan. 3, 2027, alongside the rest of the 120th Congress.

item.title: Top Dem on committee fires back after White House counsel warns against overreach amid investigation threats
item.description: White House counsel Will Scharf warns House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia against overreaching congressional authority.
item.content:encoded:
Counsel to the president William Scharf, in a letter to House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., warned against Democrats running afoul of their allotted powers pertaining to investigations and subpoenas.

But Garcia — who is poised to chair the committee next year when Democrats gain the House majority — fired back, asserting that President Donald Trump's administration is weaponizing the government.

"I write to remind you of the foundational limits that the Constitution imposes on congressional investigations and subpoenas, which you and members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress," Scharf wrote in part of the letter.

'LAWYER UP': DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Republicans suffered a drubbing during the 2026 midterms and will consequently be the minority in both chambers of Congress next year.

In a statement on Election Day last week, Garcia warned, "Lawyer up."

Rep. Emily Randall, D-Wash., who is also on the committee, declared in a post last week on the social media platform Bluesky, "We’re going to be passing out subpoenas like candy."

In his letter, Scharf asserted, "We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government. Recent public statements underscore these concerns. You and your congressional colleagues have asserted that they will issue subpoenas to harass, threaten, and deter dedicated members of the Administration from further service."

"Compulsory process is a power Congress has for oversight functions, and only for oversight functions. Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end," Scharf's letter stated.

"Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality," the letter continued. "And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation."

DEMS PIVOT FROM 'AFFORDABILITY' PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Responding to the letter, Garcia suggested in a statement that the president is hiding something from the public.

"It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let’s be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate," Garcia said in his statement.

"The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse. The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers," Garcia stated.

TRUMP ORDERS DOJ PROBE INTO DEMOCRATS OVER ALLEGED THREATS AGAINST ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Wednesday.

item.title: Trump defends Iran war during Veterans Day address, says he is making the world 'safer'
item.description: Trump told veterans at Arlington National Cemetery that the Iran conflict will end soon, vowing "total victory" in his Veterans Day address.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump defended the war in Iran and said it will be over "soon" during his Veterans Day address on Wednesday.

Trump made the statement while speaking to a crowd of veterans and their families at Arlington National Cemetery. He highlighted the 1983 Iran-backed bombing of the U.S. Marine Corps barracks in Beirut and argued that Iran has been at war with the U.S. for decades.

"America did not start a war with Iran. Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. They should have been taken care of a long time ago," Trump said.

RUBIO'S DEFENSE OF TRUMP'S IRAN WAR DRAWS SHARP CONTRAST WITH VANCE'S MIDTERM BLAME

"And it was just about time somebody fought back. All of us fought back. We fought back, and we fought back. We won. Now the question is when we want to end. We must have a total victory. Not a 93% victory. It's going to be total," he continued.

Trump noted that of the roughly seven months of conflict, "only a few weeks were active fighting," but he acknowledged the casualties America sustained.

"We lost 18 beautiful souls," Trump said. "When this conflict is over, and it will be soon, the entire world will be much safer, a better place, more peaceful place and a place without the kind of danger that we had to suffer."

TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE

Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have shied away from plans to re-escalate the conflict with Iran following the midterm elections.

Administration officials have instead pointed to economic and diplomatic solutions to the conflict.

IRAN’S DEEPEST WEAKNESS IS GETTING EXPOSED THROUGH AMERICA’S MAXIMUM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN

"We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure," Rubio told reporters on Tuesday.

He rejected the suggestion that the U.S. and Iran were at a stalemate, arguing that sanctions, the naval blockade and other measures were steadily weakening Tehran.

"They’re bleeding. They’re bleeding economically," Rubio said. "It is an increased pressure on Iran that continues to grow every day."

Fox News' Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: Veterans in Congress projected to decline, but Dems bringing more first-time vets by 3-to-1 margin over GOP
item.description: Democrats send roughly three times as many veteran freshmen to the 120th Congress as Republicans, even as overall veteran representation hits a low.
item.content:encoded:
The share of military veterans in Congress is projected to fall to its lowest level in decades in the incoming 120th Congress, but while overall veteran representation continues a long-term decline, the partisan composition of the freshman class marks a sharp contrast.

Democrats are bringing roughly three times as many first-time veteran members as Republicans, and they are catching up among House members overall.

Still, as America marks Veterans Day, the numbers show the institutional voice of military service in the legislative branch is heading toward its lowest watermark in modern history.

AFTER GOP'S BRUTAL MIDTERMS, ‘CHUCK NORRIS OF FLORIDA POLITICS’ TELLS PARTY TO 'GET UP AND FIGHT'

Analysis from With Honor Action and Military Times indicates veterans will hold roughly 15% of seats when the new Congress convenes in January, down from about 19% in the outgoing body and well below the 27% recorded in 2001 before the war on terror began. That comes despite a record number of veterans running in 2026, according to the analysis.

In January 2025, there were just 28 Democrats compared to 72 Republicans, according to Military Times. Among the 79 projected for the 120th Congress, the partisan gap is closing to 33 Democrats and 46 Republicans.

In addition to the massive Republican midterm losses, at least 11 Democratic veterans are projected to win House seats for the first time.

One uncalled race between Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., and her Democratic challenger, retired Navy Rear Adm. Eileen Laubacher – a former longtime Republican who switched parties in 2024 – remains in Colorado’s 4th District. Laubacher holds a roughly 3,300-vote lead with nearly all ballots counted. Some outlets have called the race for Laubacher, an outspoken critic of War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

DEMOCRATS FAR LESS LIKELY THAN REPUBLICANS TO PRIORITIZE PATRIOTISM AS KEY VALUE, POLL FINDS

Among the confirmed Democratic freshmen are former Navy Vice Adm. Nancy Lacore, D-S.C., who was removed from her post as chief of the Navy Reserve by Hegseth in August 2025.

Other Democratic veterans entering Congress as freshmen, as first reported by National Interest:

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

Several of these Democrats have criticized Hegseth’s personnel decisions, promotion interventions and focus on cultural issues, with some signaling support for heightened oversight or impeachment proceedings. Lacore, the highest-ranking veteran in the new class, has said she was never given a reason for her firing and has argued that Hegseth’s leadership has damaged military readiness.

On the Republican side, four first-time veteran members are heading to Washington:

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

These Republicans have generally aligned with the administration on defense priorities, including support for Hegseth.

The decline in veteran membership in Congress includes 12 Republicans defeated this year:

GOP LAWMAKER SAYS MORE QUALIFIED OFFICIALS SHOULD LEAD PENTAGON, QUESTIONS HEGSETH'S 'MORAL COMPASS'

Among the veterans who retired or did not seek re-election, it was largely Republican (11) versus Democrat (2):

HEGSETH RIPS IMPEACHMENT PUSH FROM OUTGOING REPUBLICAN AS 'FARCE, ' 'STUNT'

Three leave Congress after running for another office and losing:

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Four Republicans and one Democrat left office early in the past Congress or died.

item.title: Hegseth could face new impeachment push over Ukraine aid, lawmakers warn
item.description: War Secretary Pete Hegseth could face new articles of impeachment over Ukraine military aid as House Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Some House Democrats are leaving the door open to additional articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of military aid to Ukraine, according to lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital after a failed impeachment effort led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie.

But a conservative legal expert suggested the renewed impeachment push may be less about removing Hegseth from office than discouraging conservatives from serving in future Republican administrations.

Massie, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital that while he could not substantiate allegations that Hegseth improperly withheld military assistance to Ukraine, he believes Democrats will investigate the matter and potentially introduce additional articles of impeachment when they take control of Congress in January.

"I believe [Democrats] may use some of the same articles of impeachment when they're in the majority, but I also believe there are gonna be some other articles of impeachment based on hearings and committees," Massie told Fox News Digital. "I think the Democrats will do that."

DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY

"I heard that as one of the complaints that wasn't in my impeachment resolution," Massie added.

Massie acknowledged that another impeachment effort could be largely symbolic if the Senate fails to convict Hegseth, but argued that the proceedings could still pressure the war secretary to resign.

While impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority in the Senate.

Massie said he hopes a Democratic-controlled Senate would hold a trial if the House impeaches Hegseth.

"So there's still a reason to proceed," Massie said.

His remarks came after the House rejected his effort Tuesday to impeach Hegseth over military operations against Iran and suspected drug smugglers in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans without congressional authorization.

The Constitution grants Congress the power to declare war, while the president, as commander in chief, has authority to direct military operations. The extent to which a president can initiate hostilities without congressional authorization remains legally disputed.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., also called on the House Monday to impeach Hegseth and urged the Senate to hold a trial to remove him from office.

Schumer did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Zach Smith, a legal fellow at the Heritage Foundation, criticized Democrats' plans to pursue impeachment and potential prosecution of Trump administration officials, calling the efforts an "unfortunate waste of time" given the two-thirds Senate majority required to convict and remove an impeached official.

Smith argued, however, that Democrats are prioritizing impeachment proceedings to discourage conservatives from serving in future Republican administrations, not to actually remove Hegseth. 

He added that the efforts would also divert congressional attention from "the many very important issues that our country is facing today," including concerns Democrats campaigned on ahead of the midterm elections, such as driving down the cost of living. 

"Not only does this mean that the House and the Senate will have to take time away from the legislative activities they should be focusing on, but it will also make it more difficult for members of the Trump administration to do their duties as well, because they'll have to be dealing with these requests and other efforts by Congress," Smith told Fox News Digital.

Despite Smith's concerns, Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., echoed Massie's expectations, telling Fox News Digital that she anticipates congressional oversight committees will investigate Hegseth's handling of military assistance to Ukraine.

Grijalva said she expects congressional committees to hold hearings examining Hegseth's handling of Ukraine funding.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

"This is an issue that will come up again, because once we have more information into how bad his handling has been, we will likely have more movement and possibly more articles of impeachment," Grijalva told Fox News Digital.

The Arizona Democrat, who described herself as "a big believer in process and getting the facts out," argued that voters sent a clear message during the 2026 midterm elections.

Grijalva said Americans spoke "very clearly" when they voted, signaling that "they want to put an end to the corruption."

Fox News Digital could not independently verify the allegation that Hegseth improperly withheld Ukraine funding or engaged in any wrongdoing related to the matter.

Hegseth did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., told Fox News Digital that he had "no idea" whether additional impeachment articles would be introduced and was unaware of evidence supporting the allegations. However, he expressed support for removing Hegseth from office.

"I will fully support impeaching him," Wiener told Fox News Digital. "He's a disaster to our military and our country."

Republicans, meanwhile, accused Democrats of pursuing politically motivated impeachment proceedings against Trump administration officials.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital following Tuesday's vote that he was "not surprised" by Democrats' interest in impeaching Hegseth.

Mast argued that Democrats were determined to impeach "anyone who was appointed by the president," regardless of whether evidence supported the allegations.

The discussions come as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, giving the party greater power to launch investigations, hold hearings and pursue impeachment proceedings.

item.title: Ilhan Omar appears clueless on basis for federal probes: ‘You probably have more details on that’
item.description: Ilhan Omar told reporters she was never informed what federal agencies are specifically investigating, even questioning if multiple probes exist.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., told Fox News Digital on Tuesday she was never informed by federal agencies of the grounds on which she is being investigated — even claiming she isn’t sure how many probes into her there are.

"No, no," she said when asked if she had been told exactly the basis for the investigations.

There are two known ongoing federal probes into the Somali-born congresswoman — the first, confirmed by sources to Fox News Digital, is the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) looking into whether her immigration paperwork was fraudulently filled out by herself or her father; and the second is investigating her financial disclosures discrepancies and was confirmed publicly by U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro.

ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS

On Omar’s first day back on Capitol Hill following the investigations, she told Fox News Digital she doesn't know if DHS and the Department of Justice (DOJ) are each investigating her independently.

"I’m not sure," Omar said. "You probably have more details on that."

The congresswoman's feigned innocence on the matter came after she had a two-hour meeting with her lawyers at her Capitol Hill office on Tuesday.

The news of the federal investigations first gained steam after Fox News Digital first reported that agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) were executing a federal raid on Omar’s Washington, D.C., residence on Oct. 12. Sources confirmed the search was in relation to an investigation into Omar's immigration paperwork.

The Somali-born lawmaker arrived in the U.S. in 1995 as a refugee fleeing civil war after spending four years in a refugee camp in Kenya.

ILHAN OMAR HUDDLES WITH HER DC-BASED LAWYERS DURING HER FIRST DAY BACK ON CAPITOL HILL AMID FEDERAL PROBES

Federal agents reportedly seized the congresswoman’s cellphone, passport and computer. Fox News Digital also later confirmed that a sample of the congresswoman’s DNA was also obtained during the raid.

Omar told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that "most" of the items seized during the raid have been returned to her possession.

"I’ve gotten most of them back," Omar said.

More information continues to come to light as the investigations proceed, including a federal court filing identifying Omar by the name "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi," which matches the last name of her ex-husband, whom reports have alleged is her brother.

The marriage continues to draw scrutiny after the Daily Caller recently reported that her ex-husband Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, who is alleged to be her brother, described himself as a "gay man" in an academic paper that was published earlier this year.

OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE

Omar ignored Fox News Digital’s questioning about her ex-husband and rumored brother referring to himself as "gay" in Aug. 2026, just months before HSI raided her house and federal investigations got underway.

The congresswoman is still under investigation as she returns to Capitol Hill after winning re-election to represent Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District. Her two high-profile lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, were seen leaving her office in the Longworth House Office Building after a roughly two-hour meeting.

Omar’s team did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: Bernie Sanders says he won't back Schumer as push for new leadership gains steam
item.description: Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin say they will not support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, calling for a new generation of leadership.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., says he will not support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to serve as Senate majority leader once Democrats take control over the chamber next year.

Sanders was complimentary of Schumer, but said at a news conference on Tuesday that he believes "the time is now" for change in Democratic leadership.

"I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. [There’s] nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader," Sanders said at a news conference.

CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER'

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., joined Sanders at the Tuesday news conference and said she also will not be supporting Schumer. Neither has backed a specific candidate to replace Schumer, however.

"I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change," Slotkin said. "I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership … It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election."

THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL

Sanders and Slotkin join many Senate newcomers in opposing Schumer's re-election, including the likes of Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton and Troy Jackson.

A number of the more left-wing Democrats favor Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for the new leader.

SCHUMER DUCKS QUESTION ON CAMPAIGNING WITH SOCIALIST CANDIDATE WHO REFUSES TO BACK HIM AS LEADER

"I’ve said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic caucus," Van Hollen said during an appearance at Crooked Con over the weekend.

"We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers," he continued. "And that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we’re going to go."

And Van Hollen, who has previously said his focus was more on "kicking the tires" on a run for higher office in 2028, is reportedly mulling a bid for Schumer’s job, according to Politico.

Fox News' Alex Miller contributed to this report.

item.title: Multiple Kennedy family members seek to join legal battle against Trump's triumphal arch
item.description: Kennedy family members are seeking to join legal actions challenging plans to build President Donald Trump's triumphal arch, which he wants built in Washington, D.C.
item.content:encoded:
Nine members of the Kennedy family sought on Tuesday to join litigation opposing President Donald Trump's bid to build a triumphal arch in the nation's capital.

"President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes," their complaint asserted.

FEDERAL JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS CONSTRUCTION OF TRUMP'S ARLINGTON TRIUMPHAL ARCH HOURS AFTER APPROVAL

"The plaintiffs include Rory Kennedy, Maxwell Kennedy, Christopher G. Kennedy, Kerry Kennedy, Courtney Kennedy, the Hon. Kathleen Kennedy Townsend, and the Hon. Joseph P. Kennedy II, children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy; the Hon. Joseph P. Kennedy III, a grandchild of Robert and Ethel Kennedy; and Edward M. Kennedy, Jr., son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy," according to a Democracy Defenders Fund press release.

Rory and Maxwell Kennedy discussed the issue in a statement on the family's behalf.

"This action is about protecting sacred spaces that belong to the American people. Our parents, Robert and Ethel Kennedy, and our uncles, President John F. Kennedy and Senator Edward M. Kennedy, are laid to rest at Arlington National Cemetery. Our uncle Joseph P. Kennedy Jr., who lost his life serving our country in World War II, is also memorialized there. They are among the more than 400,000 veterans and family members buried or honored on this hallowed ground. We believe Donald Trump has violated the laws and procedures established by Congress to protect this most sacred national memorial. In bringing this lawsuit, we stand for those who can not stand for themselves.

LAWYER SAYS 250-FOOT TRUMP ARCH DISRUPTS HISTORIC SIGHTLINES CHERISHED BY VETERANS SEEKING BURIAL AT ARLINGTON

"Americans from every corner of the country visit Arlington to honor those who served and sacrificed for our nation. A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come. Our lawsuit asks the administration to respect the sanctity of Arlington National Cemetery, the laws established to protect it, and the rights of all Americans who come here to honor those who have served our country," the family's statement said.

Last week, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the proposed triumphal arch, shortly after a federal planning commission approved the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day temporary restraining order halting construction.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle issued this statement on Wednesday to Fox News Digital: "An activist district court has temporarily blocked the construction of the long-awaited Arch. It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery. The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation. We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds. We look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch—a tribute to 250 years of American greatness."

Trump has said the arch would be utilized for military purposes.

TRUMP SAYS NEW ARCH WILL ALSO DEPLOY DRONES, POSITION SNIPERS AND STORE AMMO

"At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch, to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," he said in a Sept. 20 Truth Social post.

Fox News Digital's Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

item.title: ‘He blamed the Jews’: GOP congressman levels explosive accusation against JD Vance over election postmortem
item.description: Rep. Randy Fine compared JD Vance's post-midterm election analysis to 1932 Germany, saying the vice president tacitly blamed Jewish people for GOP losses.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., said Vice President JD Vance's election analysis posted online last week amounted to an attack on the Jewish people, leading him to swear off support for any presidential aspirations Vance might have for 2028.

"I definitively will not be supporting the vice president in that nominating contest. I thought his message that he put out the day after the election was abhorrent and, frankly, smacked of the kind of thing you’d read in 1932 Germany," Fine, who is himself Jewish, said in an interview with Fox Now.

"He’s out in my book," he added. "He blamed the Jews for losing the election."

VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY

Fine’s blistering attack on Vance comes as the GOP is working to understand the midterm election results, in which Republicans lost control of the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate. It also underscores tensions in the GOP as the party wrestles with how to balance America-First principles with its alliance with Israel.

In his breakdown, Vance cited polling that identified four key items disillusioned voters wanted to see from Republicans: ending the war in Iran, focusing on the cost of living, putting America first and changing the U.S.-Israel relationship.

"Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats," Vance wrote.

Amid that mix, Vance especially singled out the first item, noting that Trump had himself identified the Iran conflict as a decisive factor in the midterms in interviews after the election.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said. "The president himself said so last night."

But Fine had a different diagnosis.

When asked about his comments by Fox News Digital, Fine doubled down on his characterization, arguing that the vice president had tacitly laid blame on "the Jews" in three of the four reasons he had identified.

RUBIO'S DEFENSE OF TRUMP'S IRAN WAR DRAWS SHARP CONTRAST WITH VANCE'S MIDTERM BLAME

"What does America First mean when you've said, ‘end the war’ and ‘change our relationship with Israel?’ Isn't that saying the same thing? When you hear… talk about America First, are they saying, ‘let's stop giving aid to Egypt?’ No, it's always about Israel. So it's three times out of four things," Fine said.

Although Vance’s election breakdown didn’t mention Jews specifically, Fine believes the connection between Israel as a state and the Jewish people is inseparable.

"You can't be Jewish if you don't believe in Israel. It's core to our identity and who we are," Fine said.

Fine also believes there is a distinction between Trump’s view of the war in Iran and the breakdown expressed by Vance. In particular, Fine highlighted comments from Trump in which the president said he would likely do the war over again if given the opportunity.

"The president said it himself. He said, I would do it again knowing what I know now because they can't have a nuclear weapon," Fine said.

"I'm not sure JD Vance is bothered by the idea of Iran having a nuclear weapon," he added.

Vance’s office declined to respond to the characterization.

ROBERT L MAGINNIS: IRAN WAR COST REPUBLICANS CONGRESS. WHAT WILL IT COST AMERICA?

Fine has been one of Israel’s loudest supporters in the House of Representatives. He has introduced several pro-Israel pieces of legislation, such as the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act of 2025, argued that the U.S. should recognize the Muslim Brotherhood, a political-religious organization, as a terrorist organization, and urged the U.S. to officially designate the Palestinian-controlled West Bank with the Jewish historical names of "Judea and Samaria."

He encouraged Republicans to steer clear of seeing Israel as the reason why the GOP underperformed in the midterm elections.

"If you don't identify the true reasons for the failure, you will fail again, which is why JD Vance can't be our nominee because he doesn't understand the reason that we lost the election," Fine said.

item.title: Moderate Dem governor-elect in hot seat after signaling one of her 'top priorities' in presser: 'Resist'
item.description: Amy Klobuchar's push for Minnesota gun safety legislation drew fierce conservative backlash over a bill that would ban AR-15 sales and limit magazines.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Governor-elect Amy Klobuchar, who has positioned herself as a moderate during her years in Congress, is facing blowback over comments made shortly after the election suggesting she will push for gun control when she takes office.

"The gun safety bill is going to get passed, and I am so excited to be working with the leaders on this, and it certainly should be one of our top priorities," Klobuchar said during a press conference. "I think that bill makes a lot of sense. I’m sure that we’ll make some changes … but the basics of that bill I hope will remain in place."

The bill Klobuchar referenced is SF 4067, an omnibus gun-control package that passed the Minnesota Senate 34-33 earlier this year but has not received a House vote. The measure would prohibit federally licensed firearms dealers from selling certain semiautomatic military-style assault weapons, including AR-15s, as well as large-capacity magazines capable of holding more than 17 rounds.

The legislation would allow current owners to keep the covered firearms and magazines, but require them to obtain an ownership certification from the state Bureau of Criminal Apprehension and renew that certification every three years. Knowingly possessing an uncertified weapon or magazine would be a gross misdemeanor, with a subsequent violation punishable as a felony.

INSIDE TRUMP'S UNPRECEDENTED BATTLE PLAN TO EXPAND SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS THROUGH JUSTICE DEPARTMENT

Klobuchar quickly faced criticism from conservatives and pro-Second Amendment groups on social media, accusing her of pushing a liberal gun control agenda on law-abiding Minnesotans, particularly in rural areas.

"Democrats don't care about affordability. They only care about taking away our Second Amendment rights," conservative communicator Steve Guest posted on X. "Amy Klobuchar can't contain her excitement as she goes after law-abiding gun owners."

"In one of her first acts as governor-elect, Sen. @amyklobuchar affirmed that she will go after Minnesotans' firearms under the guise of ‘safety,’" the National Rifle Association (NRA) posted on X.

"When Amy Klobuchar told you over and over she was going to do a top-to-bottom audit, she meant of your guns, not your tax dollars," Minnesota attorney and former immigration judge Nathan Hansen posted on X.

DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED

"Why are you babbling about gun control?" Minnesota Miners, a pro-mining grassroots nonprofit in Minnesota, posted on X. "Instead you should be coming out with your plan to stop government fraud and lowering taxes. But you can't do that you have to come out attacking & trying to violate lawful gun owners constitutional rights."

"We have a duty to our nation to not comply," Minnesota Republican state Rep. Ben Davis posted on X. "Resist."

"AMY KLOBUCHAR ISN'T EVEN SWORN IN AND SHE'S ALREADY COMING FOR MINNESOTA'S RIFLES," conservative influencer Gunther Eagleman posted on X.

Fox News Digital reached out to Klobuchar’s team for comment on what aspects of the bill she does and does not support but did not receive a response.

"I am committed as ever to moving our state forward, not moving our state to the left or to the right, but moving our state forward," Klobuchar said during the press conference.

Klobuchar, who has served as a Minnesota senator since 2007, defeated Minnesota Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth 13 points in the gubernatorial election earlier this month and will take office in January, replacing Gov. Tim Walz, who dropped his re-election bid in January amid fallout from a massive fraud scandal.

item.title: Drug ring busted, illegal aliens cuffed by Homeland Security Task Force in South Carolina: DOJ
item.description: A Homeland Security Task Force investigation in South Carolina netted 36 arrests, seizing 346 kilograms of fentanyl and $2.8 million in cash.
item.content:encoded:
The Department of Justice on Tuesday announced that dozens of people in South Carolina, including several illegal immigrants, have been arrested in relation to a drug bust and money laundering scheme.

A Homeland Security Task Force investigation netted 36 arrests — and nine of the suspects are in the country illegally, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ). The bust resulted in the seizure of 346 kilograms of fentanyl, 23 kilograms of methamphetamine, 70 kilograms of cocaine, 34 pounds of marijuana and 43 firearms.

"Nothing will stop the Trump administration’s commitment to protecting the American people from lethal drugs," Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News Digital.

DOJ ANNOUNCES 81 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS INDICTED AFTER PUERTO RICO DRUG TRAFFICKING TAKEDOWN

"Thanks to the work of the Homeland Security Task Force, the people of South Carolina are safer today than they were two years ago. The Department of Justice will continue dismantling drug trafficking networks and delivering justice for victims and their families," he added.

Investigators seized $2.8 million in cash and jewelry, 15 luxury vehicles — including two Rolls Royces, a Lamborghini and an Aston Martin — and 17 properties, which the DOJ said is worth $4 million.

The drug running operation has been ongoing since at least 2021, and the drugs themselves originated in Mexico.

The narcotics were trafficked across the U.S. southern border with Mexico and into South Carolina, according to the DOJ.

DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK

Notably, members of the ring had infiltrated the prison system in the Palmetto State.

"The investigation identified that a Mexico-based drug trafficking and money laundering organization has been operating in South Carolina since at least 2011 and its members are active in Mexico, South Carolina, other states, as well as within the Bureau of Prisons and South Carolina Department of Corrections," according to the DOJ.

The Homeland Security Task Force was assembled under Executive Order 14159, dubbed "Protecting the American People Against Invasion," and is described as a "whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad."

"Today's indictment sends a clear message that law enforcement will continue pursuing those responsible for distributing dangerous drugs and fueling criminal activity in our communities," said Michael J. Connolly, acting special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Atlanta Field Division. "This investigation reflects the dedication and coordinated efforts of our federal, state, and local partners. We will not stop at the first arrest. We will continue following the evidence, identifying those involved, and holding them accountable."

FEDS DISMANTLE ALLEGED GUN TRAFFICKING RING THAT FUNNELED DOZENS OF FIREARMS FROM GEORGIA TO CHICAGO GANGS

No fewer than 29 law enforcement agencies were involved in the investigation, including the DEA, FBI, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), state investigators in South Carolina and police departments in North and South Carolina.

item.title: New Texas governor-elect strikes conciliatory tone toward Musk after campaigning against SpaceX deal
item.description: Gina Hinojosa signaled a possible shift on the Boca Chica State Park land deal, saying Texas can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk.
item.content:encoded:
Texas’ Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is striking a more conciliatory tone toward Elon Musk after campaigning against a proposed SpaceX land deal, saying she can work with his companies if they operate "on our terms."

"As Governor, I’ll protect our land and our livelihoods – not sell out to the highest bidder – because Texans deserve a leader who puts the people first," Hinojosa said in a campaign press release in October.

But having won her election, her tone has shifted.

TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES

The governor-elect has hinted that she might be rethinking her relationship with Musk, underscoring the shifting considerations many Democrats critical of business titans are making as they prepare to govern and secure growth and investments for their constituencies.

"We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies," Hinojosa said in an interview with CNN on Thursday, just two days after election night.

"But it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that’s what changes now that I will be governor."

Hinojosa’s public land concerns center on Boca Chica State Park, a coastal reserve spanning 1,000 acres at the southernmost point of Texas. The park sits just a short distance from SpaceX’s Starbase, one of its rocket launch sites.

A possible land sale to Musk has been in the works for some time.

A Cameron County Commission agenda notice from 2024 raised a prospect presented by SpaceX: a land swap. Texas would give 43 acres of Boca Chica to SpaceX in return for 477 acres in the nearby area so that the company could expand its launch facilities.

In August 2025, the commission approved a separate proposal authorizing TPWD to sell SpaceX four noncontiguous tracts totaling about 1.9 acres.

Last year, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission voted to approve that smaller deal.

"The Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission adopts the Resolution attached as Exhibit A and authorizes the Executive Director to take all necessary steps to dispose of four tracts totaling approximately 1.9 acres at Boca Chica State Park," the commission wrote in its agenda records.

MUSK ISSUES DIRE WARNING OVER 3 MOVES DEMS COULD MAKE IF THEY SWEEP WASHINGTON: 'END OF DEMOCRACY'

During her first press conference after the election, Hinojosa didn’t rule out the project but noted that she had requested that the decision be stayed at least until she took office.

"This morning I was pleased to talk to the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife to confirm that this issue was not on today’s agenda and to request that no action be taken out of respect for this transition," Hinojosa said on Thursday.

Notably, Hinojosa bashed outgoing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott for even considering the deal with SpaceX, framing it as a capitulation to America’s wealthiest business owner.

"After 12 years of selling out Texas to his corporate donors and making working people foot the bill, Greg Abbott is handing over our land to the world’s only trillionaire. Let me be clear: Texas is not for sale," Hinojosa wrote.

"This is the One Fight that unites us all: Are we going to be a Texas by and for the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and the rest of us just live here?"

Hinojosa’s transition team did not respond to an inquiry from Fox News Digital on whether the governor-elect’s outlook had changed regarding SpaceX or its ongoing negotiations with Texas.

It also did not respond to questions about what considerations might prevent Musk from securing the 1.9 acres.

Even so, Hinojosa’s language surrounding the land sale seemed to spark blowback from Musk. In a cryptic post to social media, Musk noted that he had relocated his company to Texas because of the state’s commitment to pro-business policies.

TEXAS OVERTAKES CALIFORNIA AS 'AMERICA’S CENTER OF GRAVITY,' CLAIMS TREASURY SEC BESSENT

"SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government," Musk said in a post to X.

"As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas," he added.

Having secured her gubernatorial election win over Abbott, Hinojosa will take the oath of office on Jan. 19, 2027.

item.title: Bessent moved to military base as Iran threats exceed ‘advanced stage,’ official says
item.description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reportedly relocated to a military base as Iranian assassination plots against U.S. officials intensify.
item.content:encoded:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been relocated from his home in Washington, D.C., to a military base amid Iranian assassination threats this week, a senior administration official confirmed to Fox News.

Tehran has ramped up its efforts to target senior U.S. officials overseas, with White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also relocating to military or protected housing in recent weeks.

The senior official told Fox that threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage." The official declined to say when exactly Bessent was relocated.

Bessent has played a central role in the economic battle against Iran, launching "Operation Economic Outcast" this summer in an effort to isolate Iran's economy from the rest of the world.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

Bessent said the wave of sanctions would bring about the "asphyxiation" of Iran's economy.

The Treasury Department confirmed Bessent's departure in a statement to Fox News on Tuesday, adding that the secretary refuses to "be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats."

The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation, citing three anonymous sources.

IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

The move comes as President Donald Trump continues to seek to end the war via diplomatic means, leaning away from a return to full-scale war.

Rubio himself downplayed the possibility of re-escalating the conflict on Tuesday.

TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT

"We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure," Rubio told reporters.

He rejected the suggestion that the U.S. and Iran were at a stalemate, arguing that sanctions, the naval blockade and other measures were steadily weakening Tehran.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

"They’re bleeding. They’re bleeding economically," Rubio said. "It is an increased pressure on Iran that continues to grow every day."

The push comes a week after an election in which the war proved a political liability for Republicans.

The Iran war was a crucial factor in the House vote for 34% of voters, according to the Fox News Voter Poll, while about six in 10 said the U.S. had made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran.

Fox News' Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

item.title: FIRST ON FOX: Supreme Court justices confront what it will take to keep America's founding freedoms alive
item.description: Supreme Court justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett urged Americans to study civics education as the nation turns 250.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: As America celebrates 250 years of independence this year, three conservative Supreme Court justices are warning that preserving the nation's founding freedoms for future generations depends on Americans understanding their history, embracing civic education and actively participating in their system of government.

Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett each implored Americans to familiarize themselves with their system of government and the history behind it to ensure that the nation’s legacy is preserved.

Though the three conservative justices were united in their call for civic education, they each approached the topic differently in a series of interviews filmed by the Federalist Society and obtained by Fox News Digital. The videos come ahead of the Federalist Society's 2026 National Lawyers Convention this week, which spotlights "250 Years of American Exceptionalism."

Gorsuch, for instance, struck a distinctly religious tone.

GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK

"I think it's very easy to take the rights granted in our Constitution and the ideals expressed in the Declaration for granted," he said. "They are, for us, a little bit like the air we breathe and the water a fish might swim in. They seem natural to us, but they weren't in 1776. The ideas in the Declaration of Independence that all of us are created equal, that every one of us has God-given rights — they don't come from government, they come from God."

Gorsuch, who was appointed to the court by President Donald Trump in 2017 following the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, went on to describe the importance of historical study to the preservation of the American way of life.

THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER

"Our country is a blessing from God, and that we owe great thanks for it, and we have great responsibility for it," he went on. "The reason why our Constitution and Declaration have survived is because people choose it anew in every generation. You need to know its history. You need to know what you're preserving. Daniel Webster said it took 6,000 years for us to generate a system of government like this. Don't expect that to happen easily or again."

Kavanaugh, similarly, emphasized the importance of education.

"I think our education system is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that in the next 250 years, we preserve this republic and improve upon this republic. So, teaching American history, teaching the values of this country, the history of this country, why this country exists, how this country has been preserved, how this country has been improved over time, for example, by our constitutional amendment process and otherwise," the justice, appointed to the bench following a tumultuous confirmation process in 2018, said.

"And I think all of us should be constantly striving to ensure civics education, not only for our youth, but for all of us, and that we constantly are learning and participating in our system of government," he continued.

SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH

The Federalist Society filmed its interviews ahead of its National Lawyers Convention, which will bring together minds from across the conservative legal movement to discuss matters deemed pressing.

While not interviewed by the Federalist Society, Justice Sonia Sotomayor shared her thoughts on America's 250th anniversary during an event at Mount Vernon's Washington Library, taking a slightly darker tone than her conservative colleagues.

During her talk, which centered primarily on civic engagement, Sotomayor argued that the United States is in a rough place at the moment and that it would take "some hard work" for it to get back on an "even keel."

"There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means."

Barrett, meanwhile, focused on the Declaration of Independence and how she believes it should inspire civic participation today.

"We're not passive observers in the American project. We're participants in it. It is our project," she said. "I might suggest that people look at the last line of the Declaration of Independence. It ends with a mutual pledge in which the signatories to the document mutually pledge their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor to the success of the American project. And they made good on that promise. Some lost their fortune, lost their property to loyalists ... and they pledged with their honor not to deviate from the commitments that they had made in signing the Declaration of Independence."

"Surely that's the kind of commitment that it takes to have it keep going forward," said Barrett.

item.title: Senate Republicans plan 54-day blitz to push Trump's agenda before Democrats seize power
item.description: John Thune and Senate Republicans agreed to a resolution to maximize their remaining 54 days in power before Democrats take control next year.
item.content:encoded:
With their leadership elections settled, Senate Republicans are gearing up to "maximize" their remaining time in power before Senate Democrats take over next year.

All eyes are again on Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who was re-elected to another term as the Republican leader. Shortly after winning, Thune declared that he and the Senate GOP were "committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can."

"That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we're here, the number of hours we're here, the number of votes we may end up taking," Thune said. "But we are going to finish this legislative session strong."

SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE

The Senate was initially set to be in roughly 20 days from Tuesday until the changing of the guard, but Republicans are now squeezing the juice out of every last minute to ram through must-pass legislation, dozens of President Donald Trump’s nominees and more.

And Republicans agreed to hold themselves to that sprint until the end of the year at the tail end of their marathon closed-door meeting on Tuesday.

Lawmakers plan to "maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3," according to a resolution agreed to in the meeting obtained by Fox News Digital.

Another crack at budget reconciliation could be the trickiest part of their ambitious year-end gauntlet, particularly depending on what lawmakers try to cram into the process.

GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS

"I think we've got to keep it realistic to probably have any chance of passing, pretty narrow," Thune told Fox News Digital.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who chairs the Senate Budget Committee responsible for developing the scaffolding around the process, told Fox News Digital that he intended to present his plan to Republicans during their lunchtime meeting on Wednesday.

It’s also where Republicans are considering one last attempt at getting the SAVE America Act, or a version of it that could pass muster with the Senate rules referee.

"Oh yeah, that'd be part of it, you know, to provide funding for states for election integrity type of measures," Johnson said.

Defense funding will be another major task for Republicans, given that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats are determined to use Congress’ power over the nation’s purse strings as a way to choke off spending on the Iran war.

SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS

Thune acknowledged that reconciliation could be another landing spot for Pentagon dollars to flow, but hoped Democrats would choose a different route.

"It's going to depend on whether or not they have any of their members who are persuaded that making sure that we have enough munitions and ammo and weaponry to be able to defend the country is a priority," Thune said. "I hope they do, in which case maybe we won't have to go down that path, but we're scoping it out right now."

One of the White House’s top priorities, and at the top of Thune’s to-do list, is confirming a slate of judicial and executive branch nominees. As of Tuesday, there were 23 judicial nominees, many of whom still needed to go through committee, and nearly 100 executive branch nominees that need confirmation.

There is a slew of other high-priority items that were punted to the lame duck, like the National Defense Authorization Act, a bipartisan permitting reform package and keeping the government funded.

Preventing another shutdown, or at least hammering out a deal, could be tricky given how the political winds shifted after the election.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., who serves on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Fox News Digital that "where we can clear the decks, the better," to fund the government.

"I know that prior to the election that was the thought of some of our Democratic colleagues as well, but we have to be able to work together to get some of that done," Britt said.

item.title: House Dem criticizes Fetterman's record, mulls 2028 Senate bid
item.description: Democratic Rep. Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania indicated to Politico that she's thinking about potentially mounting a bid for U.S. Senate.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., is reportedly mulling a U.S. Senate bid, a move which could mean challenging Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., who would need to seek re-election in 2028 if he wants to pursue a second term.

"I’m going to be considering it," Dean said in an interview with Politico published Tuesday.

Dean expressed disappointment with Fetterman's performance as a senator.

GAZA-BORN DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST LAUNCHES PRIMARY BID AGAINST SEN JOHN FETTERMAN

"I have been concerned about, really, two things, which is his family and his health … and am very disappointed in his activity as a senator and in his votes," she noted, according to Politico.

Dean's campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's comment request on Wednesday.

BITTER FETTERMAN-EL-SAYED FEUD THREATENS TO COMPLICATE SCHUMER'S SENATE UNITY PUSH

The congresswoman, who has served in the House since early 2019, just won re-election to a fifth term.

Last year, a report quoted Dean as saying there was "no way" that she would mount a bid to challenge Fetterman.

FETTERMAN PLAYS POLITICAL MAVERICK, BUT HIS VOTING RECORD TELLS ANOTHER STORY

But she strongly criticized Fetterman after he recorded a video that played during the GOP midterm convention earlier this year.

"To me, that was a very sad stunt, that he would stand there aligning himself with the most corrupt president of our lifetime, if not the most corrupt president in history. I have said I hope John comes back to the Democratic fold," she said.

item.title: Dakota Meyer survived a battle he thought would kill him. 15 years after leaving the Marines, he went back
item.description: Dakota Meyer reenlisted in 2025 and completed reconnaissance Marine training at 38, calling it the hardest thing he's ever done in his life.
item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years after Dakota Meyer left the Marine Corps, the Medal of Honor recipient decided to put the uniform back on — becoming the first with the award to ever reenlist.

Meyer was 36. He had fought in Afghanistan, struggled with the transition home from war and spent years building a life outside the military. But he said the desire to serve never went away.

"Every day after I took that uniform off, that desire to serve didn't just end because my commitment to the country did," Meyer told Fox News Digital in an interview ahead of Veterans Day.

AMERICAN WAR HERO DETAILS DIRE LIVING CONDITIONS US TROOPS FACE AS HEGSETH TAPS HIM TO 'FIX' IT

Meyer rejects the idea that receiving the Medal of Honor meant he had already done enough.

"I think sometimes it's looked at as you've done your part, and I am wholeheartedly against that," he said. "I believe that the only time you've done your part is when you've done all that you can."

For Meyer, Veterans Day is a reminder that service does not necessarily end when someone leaves the military.

"Sometimes we look at the veteran title as it is something that represents something we've done," Meyer said. "And it's not. It's something that we are doing, and it is something that we can continue to do."

Meyer reenlisted in 2025 and later entered the training pipeline to become a reconnaissance Marine, completing the grueling course in his late 30s.

"To be able to do that at 38, it was definitely one of the — hands down — probably the hardest thing that I've ever had to do," Meyer said.

His first stint in the Marines had taken him to Afghanistan, where at 21 he fought in the 2009 Battle of Ganjgal in Kunar Province.

Meyer had been assigned to remain with the vehicles at a rally point while other members of his team accompanied Afghan troops toward the village roughly a mile away. The patrol was ambushed by more than 50 insurgents firing from fortified positions on the surrounding slopes.

MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH'

Meyer and Staff Sgt. Juan Rodriguez-Chavez could hear the battle unfolding over the radio. Four members of Meyer's team were trapped inside the ambush.

After repeatedly asking for permission to go in, Meyer and Rodriguez-Chavez drove toward the fighting, with Meyer manning the gun turret.

"I think often we try to make these decisions as if it's some heroic decision, and it's really not," Meyer said. "It's just about following through on what my promise that I had made to them."

The pair made repeated trips into the ambush, helping evacuate wounded troops as Meyer continued searching for his teammates.

"I think it was at that point that I did realize that I just accepted that I was going to die," Meyer recalled. "But I was gonna make sure that I would do everything I could up until that last breath."

His four teammates were ultimately found dead. Meyer would receive the Medal of Honor for his actions that day.

Leaving the Marines the following year brought a different battle.

"I struggled. I mean, I struggled," Meyer said. "The horrors of war definitely haunted me when I got out."

Meyer said one of the hardest parts of returning to civilian life was figuring out what could replace the sense of purpose he had found in the military.

"The hardest part was finding purpose," he said. "It wasn't about being successful in anything."

Eventually, he said, he realized that neither money nor professional success was what he was looking for. He wanted to feel that his work had an impact.

Years later, while speaking to a group of Marines at Camp Pendleton, that question of purpose came back to him in a different way.

A Marine attending a leadership course told Meyer he was deciding whether to reenlist. He had a family and could make more money outside the military, but he loved serving.

"Do you think it's still worth serving?" he asked.

Meyer said yes, but the answer bothered him.

"I felt it was one of the most unbecoming things that I had ever said back to that crowd," Meyer said, explaining that he was telling someone else to accept the sacrifices of continued service while he was free to return to civilian life.

"I told them that I would walk out of there and I would go about reenlisting, or I would never say that to anybody again."

It ultimately took Meyer about two years to return to the Marines.

Once back, he pursued a goal he had held since first seeing a Recon Marine poster in a recruiting office as a young man.

"They were the people that we were all trying to be inside of the Marine Corps," Meyer said.

At 37 and 38, keeping up physically wasn't necessarily the problem, but recovering felt different.

"What got me was the cumulative fatigue at my age," Meyer said. "These kids can recover like nothing else."

The experience also gave Meyer a close look at a generation of Marines nearly two decades younger than the one he had served alongside in Afghanistan.

He came away impressed.

"When we talk about service members or this next generation being weaker, it's absolutely not the case," Meyer said. "These kids are hands down, they will rise to the level of expectation that is set for them."

Meyer said the Marine Corps itself has changed since he left in 2010, but he viewed much of that change as necessary. He recalled younger Marines giving him an hour-long lesson on their "new language" during a break in training and said he often found himself learning from them.

"They do things a lot smarter," Meyer said. "I found myself learning a lot more from them than I did them probably learning from me."

He said today's young service members don't have a "generational problem," and said they still want the challenge, purpose and sense of belonging that drew those to serve before them.

item.title: Small-town Marine veteran refuses to back down in 16-year fight for America's forgotten heroes — and wins
item.description: Scott Stump, a Marine veteran from North Carolina, spent 16 years battling Congress and bureaucracy to build the Desert Storm memorial on the Mall.
item.content:encoded:
A Marine veteran from a small North Carolina town spent 16 years fighting to build a national memorial honoring the Americans who served in Desert Shield and Desert Storm — overcoming congressional setbacks, years of bureaucratic hurdles and a lengthy battle over its location, all while refusing to use taxpayer money to get it done.

"I'm just an average everyday American," Scott Stump told Fox News Digital. "I just felt like something had to be done to correct what I felt was a historical oversight."

What began as one veteran's determination to ensure the sacrifices of the 1990-1991 Gulf War generation were not forgotten became a 16-year undertaking that culminated in the Oct. 24, 2026, opening of the Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial on the National Mall.

Stump, who spearheaded the effort with a team of veteran volunteers, said he insisted from the beginning that the project be built without U.S. taxpayer funding, even as it required years of congressional action, federal approvals and financial support from donors.

TRUMP SIGNS ACT CLEARING THE WAY FOR MEDAL OF HONOR MONUMENT ON NATIONAL MALL

"I made the decision right off the bat that [I] was not interested in encumbering the taxpayer at all," Stump said. "This should be 100% privately funded. Just felt like it was the right thing to do."

Stump said the idea first came to him in November 2010, as the country approached the 20th anniversary of Operation Desert Storm, the U.S.-led military campaign that liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation.

He had attended veterans events where service members from other conflicts were recognized, but those who fought in Desert Shield and Desert Storm were overlooked.

SIX AMERICAN HEROES EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW THIS MEMORIAL DAY, FROM DELTA FORCE TO A WWII BOMBER CREW

"They skipped right over it, and they act like it never happened," Stump recalled.

Living in Waynesville, North Carolina, Stump had no elaborate political operation or established Washington network to carry out his vision. Instead, he assembled a team of fellow veterans who shared his belief that the conflict deserved a permanent place in the nation's history, he said.

Stump worked with then-Rep. Phil Roe, R-Tenn., and Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark., to secure the legislation necessary to authorize the memorial.

"It was kind of a ‘Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,’" Stump said, referring to the classic film about an ordinary American navigating Washington politics.

EXCAVATION SET TO BEGIN ON TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 250-FOOT TRIUMPHAL ARCH AMID LEGAL BATTLE

The legislative effort alone took roughly three and a half to four years, and Stump said he was forced to start over after legislation introduced late in one congressional session failed to advance.

He reintroduced the effort in 2013, testified before Congress in February 2014 and watched the House approve the measure in a unanimous 370-0 vote on May 28, 2014.

Stump said the Senate effort encountered additional legislative complications that threatened to derail the memorial authorization before the congressional session ended. He fought to clear the obstacle, knowing another failure could mean starting the legislative process from scratch for a third time.

The authorization ultimately passed as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2015, which President Barack Obama signed into law in December 2014.

LAWYER SAYS 250-FOOT TRUMP ARCH DISRUPTS HISTORIC SIGHTLINES CHERISHED BY VETERANS SEEKING BURIAL AT ARLINGTON

Next came the challenge of securing a location worthy of the service members the memorial would honor. Stump initially believed the site-selection process would take approximately 18 months. Instead, it stretched to 39 months, he recounted.

He said much of that time was spent educating officials and members of federal commissions about the significance of Desert Shield and Desert Storm. Some questioned whether the conflict had truly ended, he said. Others questioned whether enough Americans had died to justify a prominent national memorial.

"’There weren't enough people who died to have a memorial for this,’" Stump recalled being told during the approval process.

After initially receiving approval for a different location, Stump and his team continued pushing for their preferred site near 23rd Street and Constitution Avenue.

FEDERAL JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS CONSTRUCTION OF TRUMP'S ARLINGTON TRIUMPHAL ARCH HOURS AFTER APPROVAL

They secured approval on June 21, 2018, in an "absolute epic battle," Stump said.

"We are not interested in just something visible," Stump said, recalling the argument he made to commissioners. "But we wanted something that was visitable."

He wanted visitors to do more than pass a monument on their way to another destination. He wanted them to walk through the memorial, experience its design and leave inspired to learn about a war that had faded from the memories of many Americans.

Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, prompting President George H.W. Bush to launch Operation Desert Shield and build an international coalition. After months of military buildup, Operation Desert Storm began Jan. 17, 1991, with weeks of airstrikes before a ground offensive launched Feb. 24 drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait in approximately 100 hours.

GOLDEN EAGLES, LIONS AND A WINGED LADY LIBERTY TOP TRUMP'S PROPOSED 250-FOOT DC TRIUMPHAL ARCH DESIGNS

"You know, you have 30 some odd countries, five continents, different races, religions, creeds," Stump said. "It's a wonderful story."

Outside of the monument this month, DJ of Wisconsin told Fox News Digital his mother served in the Air Force as a nurse in the early '90s. She was never deployed overseas, but during her time, she worked with many veterans from Desert Storm.

"[The memorial] reminded me of her and her service, and just the thanks that I have both for her and for all Americans who sign a blank check for the country that can be paid for up to and including their lives. So, I'm just very thankful, and this is a good, good, humble reminder of that sacrifice," said DJ.
